title: Learning an Instrument
objective: After this level you can explain what practice does for a musician.
summary: The best Berlin student violinists reported the most solo practice. Deliberate practice is focused and feedback-driven, but practice explains only part of skill, about 21% in music.

cards.headline: Why are the best violinists better than the rest?
cards.body: In 1993, psychologists put that question to a Berlin music academy. They grouped violin students as the best, the good, or future music teachers, and asked each one to estimate how much they had practiced over the years. The answer made practice famous. Then it got more complicated.

cards.headline: The best had practiced the most
cards.body: The difference showed up in the hours spent practicing alone. By age 18, the best students reported about 7,400 hours; the future music teachers, about 3,400. That's more than twice as much. The researchers, led by Anders Ericsson, concluded that practice was a big part of what separated them.

cards.headline: Not all practice is equal
cards.body: Ericsson called the key ingredient deliberate practice: effortful work designed to improve, with well-defined tasks, set at the right difficulty, and informative feedback. That's different from play. Running your favorite piece top to bottom for fun is playing. Slowing down the one bar you keep fumbling, fixing it and checking it again: that's deliberate practice.

mascot.line: Don't chase a number of hours. Find the bar you keep fumbling, and slow it down.

cards.headline: Practice matters. It isn't everything.
cards.body: Later research added a twist. A 2014 meta-analysis found deliberate practice explained about 21% of the differences in music performance. And a 2019 repeat of the Berlin study found no significant practice gap between the best and the good violinists. Practice clearly helps, and it's the part you control. It just isn't the whole story.

questions.prompt: In the 1993 Berlin study, which group of violin students reported the most hours of practice alone?

options.label: The future music teachers
options.rationale: They reported the fewest, about 3,400 by 18.

options.label: All groups reported about the same
options.rationale: The best reported more than twice the teachers' hours.

questions.explanation: By age 18 the best students reported about 7,400 hours of solo practice, against about 3,400 for future teachers.

questions.prompt: Which session best fits Ericsson's idea of deliberate practice?

options.label: Playing favorite songs start to finish for fun
options.rationale: That's play, not work designed to improve.

options.label: Slowly fixing one hard bar, with feedback
Listening to a recording while relaxing
options.rationale: Deliberate practice is effortful work on a task.

options.label: Repeating pieces you already play perfectly
options.rationale: Tasks should be set at the right difficulty.

questions.explanation: Deliberate practice is effortful work designed to improve: well-defined tasks, the right difficulty, informative feedback.

questions.prompt: From Level 38: what do the 1993 Mozart effect study and the 1993 Berlin practice study have in common?

options.label: Both showed that listening to music raises IQ
options.rationale: Only the Mozart study was about listening, and it didn't hold up.

options.label: Later studies scaled back the first claim
Both were confirmed in full by later studies
options.rationale: Pooled studies found no Mozart boost, and practice explained about 21%.

options.label: Both studied professional orchestra players
options.rationale: One studied college students, the other violin students.

questions.explanation: Pooled studies found no boost specific to Mozart, and later work found practice explained about 21% of performance differences, not the whole story.
